A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SARSteer research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and expanded supplementary material.

before.justification: v1 reports original safety and utility evaluations, component and hyperparameter ablations, and experiments on base and text-only models.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds experiments on additional models, speech variations, attacks, statistical stability, and human evaluation of the safety judge.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain text-derived refusal steering, PCA removal of the safe subspace, and layerwise inference-time activation updates. The new ablation formula and architecture description provide documentation; the alternative decompositions are experiments rather than replacements for SARSteer.

E1.justification: The original audio benchmarks and text-only evaluation are retained. Appendices B.7 and B.12 add Jailbreak-AudioBench accent, volume-emphasis, and laugh-emotion conditions, explicit PGD/Gaussian perturbations, and spoken PAIR/GCG attacks involving semantic rephrasing and adversarial suffixes. These substantially broaden evaluated input conditions.

E2.justification: v2 expands comparison beyond the original adapted prompt and steering defenses by evaluating the audio-specific fine-tuning defense RRS in Table 11. Table 10 also adds SVD and kernel-PCA alternatives against PCA. The original AdaShield, FSD, MDSteer-h2s, and MDSteer-c2r comparators remain.

E3.justification: The original main-table settings remain, including 100 calibration pairs, alpha=0.1, and k=10. New protocols evaluate four additional LALMs, train RRS with 100 samples, conduct a blinded stratified human study of 500 responses, and test 50 samples per PAIR/GCG attack. CKA and per-sample alignment measurements are also introduced.

E4.justification: Beyond retained component, prompt, and hyperparameter ablations, v2 adds decomposition alternatives, speech and attack robustness tests, quantitative representation comparisons, human-judge error analysis, and individual-sample selectivity analysis (B.5 and B.7–B.13). These investigate substantial additional questions about mechanism and reliability.

E5.justification: v1 does not report repeated-run counts or uncertainty estimates. v2 identifies default seed 42 and adds a five-seed study with individual results, means, and variances. It also reports human–judge agreement and Cohen's kappa, plus standard deviations, Welch's t-test, and Cohen's d for sample-level alignment.

E6.justification: Tables 1–9 and the existing plotted results are retained, while Tables 10–18 add substantial new outcomes. For example, Table 13 reports MiDashengLM Figstep ASR of 12.80% versus 0.00% and BRR of 57.20% versus 53.20%, comparing No Defense with SARSteer. Table 17 adds Kimi-Audio PAIR ASR of 58.0% versus 10.0%.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4's local-linearization derivation is unchanged. New Appendix B.13 mathematically defines a per-sample activation-alignment proxy and argues that it indicates the refusal-logit effect. This is a limited addition to the mathematical reasoning, although the connection to the gradient-dependent logit change is not established.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement replace 'the first inference-time defense framework' with 'an effective inference-time defense framework.' The central methodological contribution and claims about reducing harmful responses while preserving utility remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of the architectural modality gap, nonlinear decomposition failure, data-limited RRS performance, attack transfer, judge bias, and sample-level selectivity. B.11 additionally interprets reported ASR as an upper bound and safety gains as underestimated, although its confusion matrix does not establish strictly one-sided errors or those general conclusions.

D1.justification: v2 announces code and constructed-dataset release and supplies an access location absent from v1. It also adds architecture details, an explicit formula for the existing projection ablation, clarification of shared calibration data, defense runtimes, and attack construction parameters. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to the original method.

R1.justification: v2 acknowledges RRS and ALMGuard as existing audio-safety approaches and narrows its novelty positioning. It adds references supporting the new attacks, models, and PCA discussion, and removes the Qwen-audio 2023 citation. The broader related-work organization and LLM/LVLM positioning remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained, with localized editing and expanded explanations. The contents list becomes a descriptive appendix guide, Section 5.5 supplies an appendix pointer, and an Impact Statements paragraph is added. The additional scientific sections do not constitute wholesale rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 converts the main text and references to a two-column ICML layout and substantially rearranges and resizes figures and tables. Figure 3 gains an explicit PCA block and expanded caption, and Tables 10–18 are added. The new layout also retains a repeated template heading, 'Submission and Formatting Instructions for ICML 2026.'

improvement.justification: Five-seed results and a blinded human check of the safety judge address important stability and evaluation-reliability gaps in v1. Additional models and attack conditions substantially strengthen evidence about generalization, while release information improves reproducibility. New interpretations remain problematic: B.11 does not establish ASR upper bounds, and B.13 does not validate activation alignment as a logit-effect proxy. These weaknesses limit the added claims, but the stronger empirical validation provides a substantial net improvement.
